definition: The mix of soil, climate, slope, and farming that gives a wine its sense of place.
A second fermentation that turns sharp malic acid into softer lactic acid — the reason many reds and some Chardonnays feel creamier.
A blend, or a special lot, often used for sparkling wine and house bottlings.
A legally defined growing area. Temecula Valley AVA is the one that covers most local tasting rooms.
A measure of sugar in grapes at harvest, used to estimate potential alcohol.
American Viticultural Area — the U.S. version of an appellation. Temecula Valley is one; smaller nested AVAs exist elsewhere in California.
The drying grip from grape skins, seeds, and oak. Helps reds age and pair with steak.
The bright, mouth-watering structure in wine. High-acid whites feel crisp; low-acid wines can taste flabby.
Sugar left after fermentation. Dry wines have very little; off-dry and dessert wines keep more.
Little to no leftover sugar. Dry does not mean bitter — it means not sweet.
A hint of sweetness, common in some Riesling, Gewürztraminer, and many crowd-pleasing rosés.
How heavy the wine feels — light like skim milk, medium, or full like cream. Alcohol, extract, and oak all add body.
The flavors that linger after you swallow or spit. A long finish is usually a compliment.
What you smell. Most of “taste” is actually aroma.
Aromas that develop with bottle age, as opposed to the fruit you smell in a young wine.
The streaks that run down the glass after a swirl. They hint at alcohol or sugar, not automatically at quality.
The harvest year on the label. In Temecula, heat and harvest timing can make vintages feel quite different.
A wine named for its grape — Cabernet, Syrah, Viognier. In the U.S., it usually means that grape is the majority of the bottle.
More than one grape in the bottle, on purpose. Rhône-style and Bordeaux-style blends are common in Temecula.
A marketing phrase for older plantings. Not legally defined in California, so ask how old and why it matters.
The winery grew the grapes and made the wine at the same location, within the same AVA.
Aged on the spent yeast (lees), which can add texture and a faint bread-dough note — common in sparkling and some whites.
Dead yeast cells after fermentation. Stirring them (bâtonnage) can make a wine creamier.
Stirring the lees in barrel or tank to build texture.
Barrel aging that can add vanilla, spice, toast, and tannin. New oak is louder; used oak is quieter.
Barrels already used enough times that they add texture more than vanilla flavor.
Fermenting or aging without oak, to keep fruit and freshness — typical for many Sauvignon Blancs and rosés.
Pushing the floating grape skins back into the juice during red fermentation, to extract color and tannin.
Circulating juice over the cap of skins during red fermentation — another way to extract color.
Time the juice spends with skins. Longer usually means more color and tannin.
Holding crushed grapes cold before fermentation, aiming for color and aroma without harsh tannin.
Whole berries fermenting in a CO₂-rich tank. Often makes juicy, low-tannin reds (think Beaujolais style).
Wine with distilled spirit added. Port-style and some dessert wines.
Wine with bubbles. Méthode traditionnelle ferments in the bottle; Charmat ferments in a tank.
The Champagne method: second fermentation in the bottle, then riddling and disgorging.
Removing the frozen yeast plug from a sparkling bottle after riddling.
The small amount of wine-and-sugar added after disgorging sparkling wine, which sets how dry it tastes.
A dry sparkling style. Brut Nature is even drier; Extra Dry is, confusingly, a bit sweeter than Brut.
Pink wine, usually from red grapes with short skin contact. Not a grape — a style.
“Bleeding” juice off red grapes early. That juice can become rosé; the remaining red gets more concentrated.
When grapes change color on the vine — green to gold or purple — a visible sign that harvest is coming.
The leaves and shoots. Managing the canopy controls sun, shade, and air flow on the fruit.
Watering vines. In Temecula’s dry climate, most vineyards irrigate; how much is a farming choice.
Vines grown with little or no irrigation, where soils and rainfall allow. Rare as a pure practice in inland Southern California.
The underground vine that the fruiting variety is grafted onto, chosen for soil, pests, and vigor.
A selected version of a grape variety. One Cabernet clone can ripen differently from another in the same vineyard.
When skins and seeds are ripe, not just when sugar is high. Important in a warm valley so tannins don’t taste green.
How long grapes stay on the vine after they look ripe. Extra time can build flavor — or raisin the fruit if it gets too hot.
Removing leaves, raisined berries, and unripe clusters before fermentation.
Fermenting some or all of the grape bunches with stems. Can add spice and structure.
Pouring wine off its sediment, or giving a young tannic red air. Not every bottle needs it.
Tainted by TCA — wet cardboard, muted fruit. Not the same as bits of cork in the glass.
Too much air. Nutty, sherry-like, fruit gone flat. Sometimes intentional (oloroso); usually a fault in table wine.
Too little air during aging. Can smell like struck match or rubber, and often blows off with a swirl.
Brettanomyces yeast. A little can add leather; a lot smells like barnyard. Taste is personal.
A vinegar or nail-polish note when acetic acid or ethyl acetate get high. A little can lift aroma; too much is a fault.
Harmless crystals or color bits in an aged bottle. Decant if you don’t want them in the last glass.
Potassium bitartrate crystals — “wine diamonds.” Harmless, more common in whites that weren’t heavily cold-stabilized.
Alcohol by volume. Warm-climate wines, including many Temecula reds, often sit on the higher side.
A spirits scale (twice the ABV). Wine uses percent alcohol, not proof.
A trained wine server and buyer. Helpful in restaurants; not required to enjoy a Temecula tasting room.
A set of small pours, usually 4–6 wines, so you can compare without ordering full glasses.
The amount in the glass. Tasting-room pours are smaller than a restaurant glass — that’s normal.
Using the dump bucket. Professionals do it so they can taste more than two rooms without the drive home becoming a problem.
The vessel for leftover wine and spit. Using it is polite, not rude.
The fee a restaurant charges if you bring your own bottle. Ask before you pack one.
An older vintage the winery held back. Often poured at a premium or sold from a special list.
Bottles allocated to wine-club members, sometimes with a tasting discount or release party.
A winery’s higher-end lot. Not a legal term in California — quality varies by producer.
Bottled without filtration. Can look a little hazy and may throw more sediment.
A loose label for low-intervention winemaking. There is no single U.S. legal definition — ask what they actually did.
Farming (and sometimes winemaking) under organic rules. “Made with organic grapes” is not the same as a fully organic wine label.
A broad claim about farming and winery practice. Look for a certification if the word matters to you.
Producers who champion Syrah, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Viognier, and related grapes — a style you’ll meet often in Temecula.
Grenache, Syrah, and Mourvèdre blended together, a southern Rhône idea that Temecula does well in the heat.
An aromatic white grape — stone fruit and flowers — that likes warm days and shows up a lot in this valley.
Spain’s great red grape; several Temecula estates bottle it as a warmer-climate alternative to Cabernet.
A ripe, often jammy red (and the grape behind White Zinfandel). Handles heat; can run high in alcohol.
A dark, tannic red, not a “small Syrah.” Inky color, blackberry, and a firm grip.
Chianti’s grape — cherry, herbs, and acidity. A few Temecula rooms pour Italian-leaning bottlings.
A sweet, fortified red modeled on Portuguese Port, often poured as a last taste.
Dessert wine from grapes frozen on the vine. True ice wine is rare in Temecula’s climate; late-harvest is the local cousin.
Grapes picked extra ripe, often for a sweeter wine. Easier to make here than ice wine.
Noble rot that concentrates grapes for some dessert wines. Not a Temecula specialty, but you’ll see the word on imported bottles.
Same vintage, different wines or vineyards — comparing producers, not years.
The same wine across several vintages, to see how a site and a house change with the year.
Both can seal a good wine. Screw caps are not a quality insult; they reduce cork taint.
The air gap in a bottle. A very large gap in an old bottle can mean the seal has leaked.
Most reds are better slightly cool, not room-hot. Patio 85°F will mute a wine; a few minutes in an ice bucket helps.
